'''Atriplex semibaccata''', commonly known as '''Australian saltbush''', '''berry saltbush''', or '''creeping saltbush''', is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Amaranthaceae]] and is [[endemic]] to Australia. It is a [[Perennial plant|perennial]] [[Herbaceous plant|herb]] native to [[Western Australia]], South Australia, Queensland and New South Wales, but has been introduced into other states and to overseas countries. It flowers and fruits in spring, and propagates from seed when the fruit splits open. This species of [[saltbush]] is adapted to inconsistent rainfall, temperature and humidity extremes and to poor soil. It is used for  rehabilitation, medicine, as a [[cover crop]] and for [[fodder]]. Its introduction to other countries has had an environmental and economic impact on them.

==Description==
''Atriplex semibaccata'' is a [[taproot]] [[Perennial plant|perennial]] herb, that has prostrated and [[Glossary of botanical terms|decumbent]] characteristics.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Pasiecznik|first=Nick|date=2021-04-14|title=Atriplex semibaccata (Australian saltbush).|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1079/fc.7903.20210113991|access-date=2021-05-17|doi=10.1079/fc.7903.20210113991|s2cid=240877407 |url-access=subscription}}</ref> Native to Australia and widespread in all mainland Australian states, ''A. semibaccata'' thrives in harsh and saline conditions. ''A. semibaccata'' is often mat-forming or semi-erect and can grow 40–80 cm tall, spanning a diameter of 1.5-2m. Its slender branches arise from a woody taproot.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|title=Flora of Victoria|url=https://vicflora.rbg.vic.gov.au/flora/taxon/b0c88d5d-ba8f-40b8-b5a4-e3a610171742|access-date=2021-05-17|website=vicflora.rbg.vic.gov.au}}</ref>

Leaves are white scruffy, [[Sessility (botany)|subsessile]] (small stalk) and are [[Glossary of leaf morphology|spatulate]] or [[Glossary of leaf morphology|obovate]] (oblong or elliptic) when the plant is young.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1">{{Cite web|last=Barrett-Lennard|first=E|date=2020|title=Saltbushes for dryland salinity management in Western Australia|url=https://www.agric.wa.gov.au/soil-salinity/saltbushes-dryland-salinity-management-western-australia#creepingsbush.|url-status=live|website=Agriculture and Food. Agric.wa.gov.au|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210517115904/https://www.agric.wa.gov.au/soil-salinity/saltbushes-dryland-salinity-management-western-australia |archive-date=17 May 2021 }}</ref> Leaves develop a green to grey-green colour, with a length of 5-30mm and a width of 2-9mm, where the base is tapered and tip obtuse. Leaves are thin, oblong-elliptic, obtuse and have short [[Petiole (botany)|petiolate]] (1–2 cm).<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":3">{{Cite book|last=Harden|first=G|title=Flora of New South Wales (Rev. ed.)|publisher=UNSW University Press|year=2000}}</ref> [[Stamen|Staminate flowers]] are tiny, terminal and 1.5mm wide, whereas [[Glossary of botanical terms|pistillate flowers]] cluster distally from leaves. ''A. semibaccata is'' monoecious.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":4">{{Cite journal|last=Cunningham|first=G. M|title=Plants of Western New South Wales|journal=CSIRO Publishing}}</ref>

Fruiting bracteoles are red or orange when mature, as well as having a convex and [[Rhombus|rhombic shape]] (diamond like appearance). Fruits are [[Succulent plant|succulent]], united at base, margin toothed, sessile and are a length of 4-6mm.<ref name="fao">Heuzé V., Thiollet H., Tran G., 2016. Creeping saltbush (Atriplex semibaccata). Feedipedia, a programme by INRA, CIRAD, AFZ and FAO. https://www.feedipedia.org/node/183</ref><ref name=":1" />

''A. semibaccata'' is [[Plant propagation|seed propagated]] and seeds are [[List of polymorphisms#Heterospermy|dimorphic]]. Black seeds are 1.5-1.7mm, while brown seeds are 2mm in size. It can be used as [[fodder]] and is useful for [[Land degradation|degraded]] or salt affected land.<ref name=":0" /> Optimal conditions for habitat, include dry/subtropical climate and direct sunlight. ''A. semibaccata'' has an all-year season of interest and a [[Hardiness (plants)|plant hardiness]] zone of 4. ''A. semibaccata'' requires light [[wikt:hydration#Noun|hydration]] in soil that is either [[clay]], [[loam]], [[peat]], [[sand]] or silt as well as a [[soil pH]] that is [[PH|neutral]].<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" /><ref name=":4" />

== Taxonomy and naming ==
[[File:Starr-151214-0102-Atriplex semibaccata-fruiting leaves-Near Lua Kealialalo-Kahoolawe (26284992665).jpg|thumb|224x224px|Succulent red fruits of ''A. semibaccata'' (also referred as bracteoles)]]''Atriplex semibaccata'' was first formally described in 1810 by [[Robert Brown (botanist, born 1773)|Robert Brown]] in his ''[[Prodromus Florae Novae Hollandiae et Insulae Van Diemen]]''.<ref name="APNI">{{cite web|title=''Atriplex semibaccata''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/545690|publisher=APNI|access-date=29 May 2021}}</ref><ref name="R.Br.">{{cite book|last1=Brown|first1=Robert|title=Prodromus Florae Novae Hollandiae|date=1810|location=London|page=406|url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/21771#page/276/mode/1up|access-date=29 May 2021}}</ref> The species is classified in the [[Amaranthaceae]] family and Chenopodiaceae subfamily, along with other [[Halophyte|halophytic plants]] (salt-tolerant) species. ''A. semibaccata'' has several reported varieties such as var. ''melanocarpa'', var. ''biformis,'' var. ''microcarpa'' var. ''[[Atriplex gracilis|gracilis]]'' and var. ''appendiculata''.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":19">{{Cite journal|last=Duretto, M. F., & Morris, D. I. (2011) 97 AMARANTHACEAE. Flora of Tasmania.|first=M. F|date=2011|title=97 AMARANTHACEAE - Flora of Tasmania|journal=Tasmanian Herbarium, Tasmanian Museum & Art Gallery}}</ref> These variations include the [[Plant morphology|morphological]] differences within this species.

Australia's [[Flora of Australia|native]] range is centred on bracteoles, which are the succulent fruits of ''A. semibaccata.''  There are two forms of ''A. semibaccata'' in Australia. In [[Western Australia]] and southern arid areas are home to rhomboid and succulent bracteoles, whereas slim dry and deltoid shaped bracteoles are found in [[Queensland]] and [[New South Wales]].<ref name=":5">{{Cite book|last=Australia. Bureau of Flora, & Australian Biological Resources Study.|title=Flora of Australia (Vol. 4)|publisher=CSIRO|year=1981}}</ref> ''A. semibaccata'' [[Hybrid (biology)|hybridises]] with Atriplex spinibractea, where both species subside in New South Wales. This formed the variant, known as A. neurivalvis in [[North Queensland|northern]] Queensland, where succulence is not apparent in its bracteoles.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2" /><ref name=":5" />

[[Genetic variability]] analysis with the use of [[molecular marker]]s has investigated ''A. semibaccata'' and other species of the genus ''Atriplex''. [[Phylogenetic analysis]] has confirmed a deviation from all other tested species (''[[Atriplex halimus|A. halimus]], [[Atriplex amnicola|A. amnicola]]'', ''[[Atriplex lentiformis|A. lentiformis]]'', ''[[Atriplex canescens|A. canescens]],'' ''A. undulata'' and ''[[Atriplex nummularia|A. nummularia]]'').  ''A. semibaccata'' is distinguished as one of two major groups that are least similar to the other species.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Bouda|first1=S.|last2=Del Campo|first2=F.F.|last3=Haddioui|first3=A.|last4=Baaziz|first4=M.|last5=Hernàndez|first5=L.E.|date=September 2008|title=RAPD and ITS-based variability revealed in Atriplex species introduced to semi-arid zones of Morocco|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.scienta.2008.05.033|journal=Scientia Horticulturae|volume=118|issue=2|pages=172–179|doi=10.1016/j.scienta.2008.05.033|issn=0304-4238|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Flores|first1=Hilda|last2=Davis|first2=Jerrold I.|date=July 2001|title=A Cladistic Analysis of Atripliceae (Chenopodiaceae) Based on Morphological Data|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.2307/3088719|journal=Journal of the Torrey Botanical Society|volume=128|issue=3|pages=297|doi=10.2307/3088719|jstor=3088719|issn=1095-5674|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

The common names for ''A. semibaccata'' include the ''Australia saltbush.'' It is also commonly called ''Australian saltweed, creeping [[saltbush]]'' and ''berry saltbush''.<ref name=":5" /> This is one of many ''Atriplex'' species native to Australia and is referenced widely in [[North America]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":5" /> The genus name Atriplex has [[Latin]] origins from the ‘''atriplexum''’, which has been derived from the [[Ancient greek language|Greek]] word ‘''astraphaxes''’, which translates to "''saltbush''" or "''orach''". The species [[epithet]] ‘''semibaccata''’ is derived from the Latin word ‘''semi''’ which translates to "half", while ‘''baccata''’ means "bearing berries".<ref name=":5" />

== Distribution and habitat ==

== Ecology ==

=== Reproductive biology ===
[[File:Atriplexsemibaccata.jpg|thumb|''A. semibaccata'' seed appearance and dimensions for reproduction]]''A. semibaccata'' reproduces by [[Germination|seed propagation]]. This appears when the fruiting bracteoles split when ripe and dry, exposing an individual seed.<ref name=":20">{{Cite journal|last1=Bhagwat|first1=V. M.|last2=Ramachandran|first2=B. V.|date=1975-09-15|title=Malathion A and B esterases of mouse liver-I|journal=Biochemical Pharmacology|volume=24|issue=18|pages=1713–1717|doi=10.1016/0006-2952(75)90011-8|issn=0006-2952|pmid=14}}</ref> The seed is with [[Radicle|ascending radicle]].<ref name=":5" /> ''A. semibaccata'' is self-compatible and [[Anemophily|wind pollinated]]''.''<ref name=":7">{{Cite journal|last=Le Houérou|first=H. N.|date=May 1992|title=The role of saltbushes (Atriplex spp.) in arid land rehabilitation in the Mediterranean Basin: a review|url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/BF00115408|journal=Agroforestry Systems|language=en|volume=18|issue=2|pages=107–148|doi=10.1007/BF00115408|s2cid=24377640 |issn=0167-4366|url-access=subscription}}</ref> [[Plant reproductive morphology|Male flowers]] occur as small glomerules in distal axils, while [[Plant reproductive morphology|female flowers]] appear in scattered [[Axillary bud|axillary clusters]].<ref name=":5" /> [[Seed]] persistence in soil and [[germination]] conditions are unknown. ''A. semibaccata'' does not obtain [[dormancy]] when [[germination rate]]s are high.<ref name=":7" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Mandák|first1=Bohumil|last2=Pyšek|first2=Petr|date=April 2001|title=The effects of light quality, nitrate concentration and presence of bracteoles on germination of different fruit types in the heterocarpous Atriplex sagittata: Germination of fruit types in Atriplex sagittata|journal=Journal of Ecology|language=en|volume=89|issue=2|pages=149–158|doi=10.1046/j.1365-2745.2001.00537.x|doi-access=free}}</ref>

In Australia, ''A. semibaccata'' flowers and fruits in [[Spring (season)|spring]] and [[summer]], however flowering is prolonged in Western Australia.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Atriplex semibaccata.|url=http://plantselector.botanicgardens.sa.gov.au/Plants/Details/2565|url-status=live|website=Plantselector.botanicgardens.sa.gov.au|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160805171854/http://plantselector.botanicgardens.sa.gov.au:80/Plants/Details/2565 |archive-date=5 August 2016 }}</ref> ''A. semibaccata'' in the [[Northern Hemisphere|northern hemisphere]] ([[United States|USA]]) typically flowers in spring (March–May), summer (June–August) and early [[winter]] (December–February).<ref name=":8">{{Cite journal|last1=Kadereit|first1=Gudrun|last2=Mavrodiev|first2=Evgeny V.|last3=Zacharias|first3=Elizabeth H.|last4=Sukhorukov|first4=Alexander P.|date=October 2010|title=Molecular phylogeny of Atripliceae (Chenopodioideae, Chenopodiaceae): Implications for systematics, biogeography, flower and fruit evolution, and the origin of C4 photosynthesis|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.3732/ajb.1000169|journal=American Journal of Botany|volume=97|issue=10|pages=1664–1687|doi=10.3732/ajb.1000169|pmid=21616801|issn=0002-9122|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref name=":9">{{Cite journal|last=Bullock|first=Dolores M.|date=April 1936|title=Atriplex Semibaccata as Influenced by Certain Environmental Conditions|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.2307/1931466|journal=Ecology|volume=17|issue=2|pages=263–269|doi=10.2307/1931466|jstor=1931466|issn=0012-9658|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

=== Physiology and phenology ===
The development of [[C4 photosynthesis|C<sub>4</sub>]] [[photosynthesis]] has played a role in the evolutionary success of the Atriplex genus. Various C<sub>4</sub> Chenopodiaceae plants differ from the [[Kranz Anatomy|Kranz anatomy]] of Atriplex, which includes a layer of [[bundle sheath cells]] surrounding the [[vascular bundle]], as well as radially arranged [[palisade cell]]s, with little variation in C<sub>4</sub> leaf types.<ref name=":8" /><ref name=":10">{{Cite journal|last1=de Villiers|first1=A.J.|last2=von Teichman|first2=I.|last3=van Rooyen|first3=M.W.|last4=Theron|first4=G.K.|date=October 1996|title=Salinity-induced changes in anatomy, stomatal counts and photosynthetic rate of Atriplex semibaccata R. Br.|journal=South African Journal of Botany|volume=62|issue=5|pages=270–276|doi=10.1016/s0254-6299(15)30656-6|issn=0254-6299|doi-access=free}}</ref> Depending on the immediate environmental conditions, ''A. semibaccata'' demonstrates the ability to adapt. This relates to environmental conditions such as [[air temperature]], [[soil moisture]], [[salinity]] and [[evaporation]].<ref name=":8" />

Greater exposure to a saline environment, induces a [[Abiotic stress|salt stress]] response which displays a decrease number of [[chloroplast]]s in chlorenchyma and bundle sheath cells, as well as a decreased root diameter, leaf size, [[Stromal cell|leaf stromal]] conductance and the net leaf photosynthetic rate.<ref name=":8" /> Higher saline exposure increases [[Gas exchange|intracellular CO<sub>2</sub>]] concentration and the number of stomata per unit leaf area.<ref name=":9" /><ref name=":10" /><ref name=":11">{{Cite journal|last=De Villiers|first=A. J.|date=1994|title=Ecophysiological studies on several Namaqualand pioneer species, with special reference to the revegetation of saline mined soil|journal=University of Pretoria}}</ref>

During winter, ''A. semibaccata'' becomes dormant, whereas other ''Atriplex'' species maintain function. Low and inconsistent [[rain]]fall, varying temperatures, [[humidity]] and poor soil are contributing factors that involve ''A. semibaccata'' to adapt.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Gates|first1=CT|last2=Muirhead|first2=W|date=1967|title=Studies of the tolerance of Atriplex species. 1. Environmental characteristics and plant response of A. vesicaria, A. nummularia and A. semibaccata|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1071/ea9670039|journal=Australian Journal of Experimental Agriculture|volume=7|issue=24|pages=39|doi=10.1071/ea9670039|issn=0816-1089|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

== Cultivation ==

=== Environmental requirements ===
[[File:Starr 030429-0210 Atriplex semibaccata.jpg|thumb|Growth of ''A. semibaccata'' in arid and saline conditions]]
''A. semibaccata'' is native to Australia, however it is not located in [[Tropics|tropical]] and [[Humidity|humid]] regions such as [[North Queensland|Northern Queensland]]. It is a [[drought]] tolerant species of [[Subtropics|subtropical]] arid and [[Semi-arid climate|semi-arid]] regions.<ref name=":0" /> A region with a mean annual rainfall of 250-900mm is optimal for ''A. semibaccata''. It is a low spreading and deep-rooted [[Subshrub|sub-shrub]] that does not require much [[soil moisture]].<ref name=":3" /> Sun exposed regions are an optimal condition for growth.  ''A. semibaccata'' is winter tolerant and can survive a minimum air [[temperature]] of −5 °C.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":3" /> ''A. semibaccata'' is salt-laden wind tolerant and has been indicated as an environmental advantage against plants that are distributed along [[coastal region]]s. Additionally, [[Soil salinity|saline soil]] allows for rapid and more profuse seed [[germination]].<ref name=":12">{{Cite web|first=|date=2015|title=California Invasive Plant Council|url=https://www.cal-ipc.org/|url-status=live|publisher=California Invasive Plant Council|publication-place=Berkeley, California, USA|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040511140943/http://www.cal-ipc.org:80/ |archive-date=11 May 2004 }}</ref> This is a competitive advantage, against [[native species]] worldwide.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":12" /> ''A. semibaccata'' has a high degree of salt tolerance (9-16 dS/m) and grows in soil that is exposed to light and is acidic.<ref>{{Cite web|year=2015|title=Native Seed Services|url=https://www.greeningaustralia.org.au/services-native-seed/|url-status=live|website=Florabank. Australian Government, Greening Australia|publisher=Australian Government, Greening Australia and CSIRO|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180313101739/https://www.greeningaustralia.org.au/services-native-seed/ |archive-date=13 March 2018 }}</ref>  ''A. semibaccata'' grows in various soil types, including clay loams, sandy loams and waterlogged environments.<ref name=":0" />

=== Movement and dispersal ===
Natural dispersion of ''A. semibaccata'' are over short distances as seeds are found under remnant and understorey plants. Animal dispersion expands the distance covered of ''A. semibaccata''. The red fruiting [[bract]]eoles of ''A. semibaccata'' are [[Succulent plant|succulent]] and are attractive to [[herbivore]] species.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":4" /> Species that eat the fruiting bracteoles are responsible for animal dispersion and spread the seed of A. semibaccata.<ref name=":0" /> ''A. semibaccata'' seeds have been found in the [[digestive tract]] of  [[reptile]]s, [[bird]]s and [[fox]]es in [[California]], [[United States|USA]].<ref name=":0" />  Accidental introduction of ''A. semibaccata'' is a result of relocating [[hay]] and other [[Fodder|fodder crops]]. ''A. semibaccata'' was introduced internationally to various countries, to acquire the drought and saline resistant properties that allow for use as a [[fodder]] and [[Groundcover|ground cover]]. <ref name=":13">{{Cite journal|last=Thomson|first=Linda|year=2012|title=Thomson, L. J., and C. M. Penfold. "Cover crops and vineyard biodiversity|url=https://www.wineaustralia.com/getmedia/82cd733b-fc42-46c6-89d3-298b013c341d/201207_Covercrops-and-vineyard-biodiversity.pdf|journal=Grape and Wine Research and Development Corporation, Adelaide}}</ref><ref name=":7" /> ''A. semibaccata'' is intentionally dispersed for its uses.<ref name=":0" />

== Uses ==

=== Cover crop ===
In its native range of Australia, ''A. semibaccata'' is used in [[agroforestry]] to improve the performance and [[profitability]] of [[vineyard]]s.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":13" /><ref name=":14">{{Cite journal|last=Le|first=Houérou|date=1995|title=Forage halophytes in the Mediterranean basin. In: Halophytes and biosaline agriculture|url=https://www.cabi.org/isc/abstract/19960701453|journal=CABI|isbn=0824796640}}</ref> ''A. semibaccata'' has been introduced to regions with reduced water availability due to drought and increased temperatures, as a sustainable [[cover crop]] that deters potential [[Pest (organism)|pest]] species.<ref name=":13" /><ref name=":14" /> Native [[Perennial plant|perennial]] cover crops such as ''A. semibaccata'' can increase the abundance of [[Symbiosis|symbiotic]] [[invertebrate]]s that can improve [[pest control]] and limit the need of synthetic pest controls.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":13" />

=== Rehabilitation ===
''A. semibaccata'' has been used for [[Regenerative agriculture|regenerative]] purposes, where it has been planted to restore mine spoils.<ref name=":15">{{Cite journal|last=Thomson|first=Danne|title=Effects of native grass cover crops on beneficial and pest invertebrates in Australian vineyards.|url=https://www.cabi.org/isc/abstract/20103179507|journal=Environmental Entomology|year=2010 |volume=39 |issue=3 |pages=970–978 |doi=10.1603/EN09144|pmid=20550812 |s2cid=38599721 |issn=0046-225X|url-access=subscription}}</ref> ''A. semibaccata'' is adaptive to the saline and drought conditions of [[Tailings|mining waste]] and exhibits germination among these regions.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Osborne|first=Jim|date=1995|title=Successful tree and understorey establishment on saline gold mine wastes: a preliminary overview.|journal=Mulga Research Centre Journal|issn=0818-8238}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Uyeda|first=Kellie|title=Effects of salt and drought stress on germination of non-native plants in the salt marsh to upland transition zone|journal=Estuaries and Coasts|year=2019 |volume=42 |issue=6 |pages=1686–1694 |publisher=Springer New York USA|doi=10.1007/s12237-019-00599-x|s2cid=198491671 |issn=1559-2723}}</ref> ''A. semibaccata'' has also been used for [[landscaping]] purposes and as ground cover to control soil and [[Soil erosion|erosion]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Holzworth|first=L. K.|title=A plant makes good in the southwest.|journal=Soil Conservation}}</ref>  ''A. semibaccata'' is an effective [[weed control]] in [[Road verge|verges]], [[roundabout]]s and nature strips.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2021|title=Atriplex semibaccata Berry Saltbush|url=http://plantselector.botanicgardens.sa.gov.au/Plants/Details/2565|url-status=live|website=Plant Selector|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160805171854/http://plantselector.botanicgardens.sa.gov.au:80/Plants/Details/2565 |archive-date=5 August 2016 }}</ref> Additional uses of ''A. semibaccata'' includes [[land reclamation]] without the need for saline water [[Irrigation|irrigation systems]] and restoring bare patches of ground.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Visser|first1=N|last2=Morris|first2=C|last3=Hardy|first3=Mb|last4=Botha|first4=Jc|date=2007|title=Restoring bare patches in the Nama-Karoo of South Africa|url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.2989/AJRFS.2007.24.2.5.159|journal=African Journal of Range & Forage Science|language=en|volume=24|issue=2|pages=87–96|doi=10.2989/AJRFS.2007.24.2.5.159|s2cid=83982430|issn=1022-0119|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

=== Animal feed ===
''A. semibaccata'' is used as saltland [[pasture]] and produces [[fodder]] for grazing animals when sources of paddock feed are limited. This can improve production from saltland sites, reduce salt movement and stabilise [[soil structure]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Saltland pastures in Western Australia|url=https://www.agric.wa.gov.au/soil-salinity/saltland-pastures-western-australia|access-date=2021-05-29|website=www.agric.wa.gov.au|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Frangos|first=L.G|title=Sheep and goat management.|journal=Cyprus Agricultural Journal}}</ref> ''A. semibaccata'' is a readily grazed ''Atriplex'' [[saltbush]], which provides a more diverse diet and primary fodder/ animal feed.<ref name=":0" />  The high salt content in [[Leaf|foliage]] reduces the use of ''A. semibaccata'' as a food source if availability of drinking water for [[livestock]] is not adequate.<ref name=":16">{{Cite journal|last1=Pasiecznik|first1=N.M.|last2=Vera-Cruz|first2=M.T.|last3=Harris|first3=P.J.C.|date=1996|title=The current status ofAtriplexon the Cape Verde Islands|url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0140196396901287|journal=Journal of Arid Environments|language=en|volume=34|issue=4|pages=507–519|doi=10.1006/jare.1996.0128|bibcode=1996JArEn..34..507P |url-access=subscription}}</ref> ''A. semibaccata'' is [[Palatability|palatable]] when young, contains a low energy value and is a source of [[Protein (nutrient)|crude protein]]. Additional [[food supplement]]s and adequate drinking water are necessary for livestock.<ref name=":13" /><ref name=":16" />

== Environmental impact ==
''A. semibaccata'' is grown and dispersed over short distances. This creates a dense [[Fire retardant|fire-retardant]] [[groundcover|ground cover]] that displaces [[Native species|native]] plant species.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":15" /> ''A. semibaccata'' is identified as an [[Invasive species|invasive]] species by the [[United States Fish and Wildlife Service|US Fish and Wildlife service]] and is known to affect [[endangered species]] such as [[Panicum niihauense]] (critically endangered), [[Verbesina dissita]] and [[Sesbania tomentosa]]. [[Scaevola coriacea]] and [[Sesbania tomentosa]] are native and endangered grass species of [[Hawaii]], [[United States|USA]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":12" /><ref>{{Cite web|title=The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species|url=https://www.iucnredlist.org/search?query=atriplex&searchType=species|access-date=2021-05-31|website=IUCN Red List of Threatened Species}}</ref>  Scaevola coriacea is found in three naturally occurring populations and Sesbania tomentosa is located on the island of [[Molokai]].<ref name=":0" /> In California, USA, ''A. semibaccata'' competes with native plants such as Verbesina dissita for space, shade, water and light. ''A. semibaccata'' creates an ecological shift that is caused by competition for resources, shading, ecosystem change and habitat alteration.<ref name=":16" />

''A. semibaccata'' enhances [[biodiversity]] through [[Biological pest control|biological control]]. [[Agroecosystem]]s that involve ''A. semibaccata'' increase the abundance of [[invertebrate]]s that assist in [[pest control]] as well as an increased range of [[Predation|predators]] and [[parasitoid]]s.<ref name=":11" /><ref name=":13" /> ''A. semibaccata'' acts as a [[cover crop]] that provides shelter for various invertebrates, this increases biodiversity and bioactivity. This provides the environment for natural breakdown of [[organic material]], aeration and [[Nutrient cycle|nutrient cycling]] that keeps ''A. semibaccata'' and surrounding vegetation healthy.<ref name=":13" /> Additionally, this abundant soil diversity supports pest predators that prevent harmful organisms from over populating. This prevents the destruction of crops.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":13" /> ''A. semibaccata'' improves the quality and structure of soil, suppresses [[weed]]s and contributes to pest management.<ref name=":13" /><gallery mode="packed" widths="180" heights="180">

== Economic impact ==
The economic impact of ''A. semibaccata'' is positive in regions where it is not [[Invasive species|invasive]]. Benefits that have a positive economic effect include its value in rehabilitation, [[Medicinal plants|medicinal]] properties as well as food and cover cropper. The negative economic impact is generated by its [[Invasive species|invasiveness]] that endangers [[native species]], causes a change in ecological and alters the surrounding [[biodiversity]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":12" /> This requires physical and chemical control processes that can be laborious and require economic expenditure. Control chemicals for ''A. semibaccata'' involve [[herbicide]]s, such as [[dicamba]], dicamba/MCPA amine, [[2,4-Dichlorophenoxyacetic acid|2,4-D]] and [[picloram]]/[[2,4-Dichlorophenoxyacetic acid|2,4-D]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":18">{{Cite book|last=DiTomaso|first=J.M|title=Weed Control in Natural Areas in Western United States|publisher=Weed Research and information Centre|year=2013|pages=544}}</ref>  To physically remove ''A. semibaccata'', hand pulling is an effective method due to its small size. To physically control ''A. semibaccata'', it must be uprooted prior to seed production. Site revision is required to remove plants arising from residual seed pools.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":18" />
